Title: Housing as a Human Right: Why the Government Must Seize Underutilized Private Property to End the Housing Crisis

Every person deserves a safe, stable, and dignified place to call home. Yet, in the wealthiest nations on Earth — including the United States — hundreds of thousands of people sleep on sidewalks, in cars, or in overcrowded shelters, while millions of homes sit empty, abandoned, or underused. Vacant properties clutter urban landscapes; second homes gather dust in scenic locales; and speculative investors hoard real estate as financial assets, not dwellings. This is not an accident of the market — it is a moral failure. To guarantee housing as a fundamental human right, governments must exercise eminent domain and seize privately owned vacant homes, second residences, and underutilized real estate, converting them into permanently affordable, publicly managed housing for those in need. This is not confiscation — it is justice.

The Crisis: Homes as Commodities, Not Human Needs

The housing crisis is not a shortage of physical space — it is a crisis of prioritization. In New York City alone, more than 100,000 residential units have been vacant for over a year. In Los Angeles, over 40,000 homes are unoccupied — many owned by hedge funds, foreign investors, or wealthy individuals who use them as weekend getaways. In rural America, entire towns are depopulated while luxury cabins sit untouched. Simultaneously, a family of four may wait two years for a subsidized apartment, while dying on a waiting list that never seems to move.

This is not capitalism at work — it is capitalism gone mad. When housing is treated as a speculative asset — bought, held, and sold for profit, not shelter — it ceases to be a human right and becomes a privilege reserved for the affluent. The United Nations’ 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights explicitly states in Article 25 that “everyone has the right to a standard of living adequate for the health and well-being of himself and of his family, including food, clothing, housing and medical care.” Housing is not optional. It is foundational to health, education, employment, and dignity. That millions are denied this right while thousands of properties remain unused is an intolerable contradiction that demands radical intervention.

Historical and Legal Precedent for Government Action

The power of government to seize private property for public use — eminent domain — is long-established and constitutionally protected in the United States and many other democracies. The Fifth Amendment allows for such takings provided “just compensation” is given. What constitutes “just compensation” has been interpreted consistently in courts as fair market value — not what an owner wishes the property were worth, but what a willing buyer would pay a willing seller.

Critics cry “socialism!” or “tyranny!” when this power is proposed — yet we accept it routinely for roads, schools, hospitals, parks, and even private stadiums for professional sports teams. How then can we deny this same moral and legal authority to seize vacant homes to end homelessness? If a church can be moved to make way for a highway, why can’t an empty mansion be converted into three affordable apartments? If a vacant lot can be taken to build a community center, why not a deserted townhouse?

The argument that “property rights are absolute” is a myth invented by libertarian ideologues and real estate lobbyists. Property rights have never been without limits. Zoning laws, building codes, environmental regulations, and historical preservation statutes all limit what owners may do with their land. Why should we treat housing as the one exception to all public interest obligations?

The Moral Imperative: Profiting from Human Suffering

Consider the human cost. A child sleeping in a car does not care whether their family’s homelessness is caused by lack of supply or market speculation. A veteran suffering from PTSD will not be consoled by a speech about private property. A single mother working two minimum-wage jobs should not be told her children must be raised in a shelter because a billionaire owns a ski chalet they use twice a year.

When private owners hold property empty for profit — while others die on the streets — they are not merely exercising a legal right. They are profiting from human misery. And when governments sit idle while housing prices skyrocket, wages stagnate, and homelessness soars, they are complicit. Ethical governance requires that public welfare override unproductive private accumulation when human lives hang in the balance.

Seizing underutilized real estate does not punish success — it corrects a market that has failed its most basic duty: to house people. Those who own multiple homes — particularly those never occupied or rented out — are not poor; they are affluent. They do not need to be “taken from.” They need to be reminded that wealth carries responsibility.

Practical Implementation: Fair Compensation, Public Stewardship

Opponents fear abuse, corruption, and chaos. These fears are valid — but solvable. Any property seizure program must be conducted transparently, judicially, and with fair market compensation. A neutral appraisal board — not the government — determines value. Owners receive payment within 90 days. Appeals are guaranteed. Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of implementing a policy where the government confiscates privately owned vacant or underutilized properties to provide guaranteed housing for the homeless and poorly housed population.
Model Response:

The policy of government confiscation of privately owned vacant or underutilized properties to provide guaranteed housing for the homeless and poorly housed population is not currently implemented in most democratic nations in the form of outright confiscation (i.e., seizure without compensation), but it is conceptually similar to mechanisms like eminent domain for public use, vacancy taxes, compulsory purchase, or housing redistribution under social emergency laws. When proposed or discussed in academic, activist, or policy circles, the rationale and supposed benefits are grounded in ethical, economic, and social justice arguments. Below is a detailed explanation of the reasons and proposed benefits:

Reasons for Implementing Such a Policy

1. Human Right to Housing

— The United Nations recognizes adequate housing as a fundamental human right (Article 11 of the ICESCR). When thousands of people sleep on streets or in shelters while hundreds of thousands of homes stand empty, proponents argue that the state has a moral and legal duty to intervene to uphold this right. — The juxtaposition of homelessness and vacant properties is seen as a moral failure of the market to serve basic human needs.

2. Market Failure and Speculative Vacancy

— In many urban areas, real estate is treated as a speculative asset rather than a social good. Investors or owners may leave properties vacant to:

  • Avoid renovation costs
  • Wait for property values to rise
  • Avoid renting to low-income tenants due to stigma or perceived risk — This behavior distorts the housing market, suppresses supply, inflates prices, and exacerbates inequality.

3. Inefficient Use of Resources

— Vacant homes represent wasted infrastructure: land, bricks, plumbing, electricity networks, and community services. Confiscating and repurposing them is seen as a more efficient use of existing resources than building new housing from scratch.

4. Public Emergency

— Homelessness is a public health crisis, linked to higher rates of mortality, disease transmission, mental illness, and emergency service utilization. Governments spend substantial sums on crisis response (e.g., shelters, hospital ERs, police interventions). Repurposing vacant homes is viewed as a preventative, cost-effective intervention.

5. Social Justice and Reducing Inequality

— Wealth inequality often correlates with housing inequality. A small percentage of property owners hold vast portfolios, while others struggle to pay rent or afford a home. This policy is framed as a corrective measure against systemic inequity. — It challenges the notion that private property rights are absolute, arguing that property carries social obligations.

6. Legal Precedents Globally

— Several countries already limit or penalize vacancy:

  • Spain: Vacant homes in urban areas can be forcibly rented to the public sector under “social interest” provisions.
  • Germany: Some cities impose high vacancy taxes and can compel owners to rent out units.
  • France: “Right to Housing” law (DALO) allows courts to order the state to find housing for vulnerable people, sometimes using vacant public or private property.
  • Venezuela, Cuba, Brazil: Have laws allowing state seizure or use of idle property for housing, though often controversial and inconsistently applied.

Supposed Benefits of the Policy

Benefit Explanation
Immediate Reduction in Homelessness Converts underused assets into habitable units quickly, bypassing long construction timelines.
Cost Efficiency Significantly cheaper than building new social housing. Renovating an empty house can cost 1/3 to 1/2 the price of new construction.
Urban Revitalization Occupied homes reduce blight, crime, and vandalism in neglected neighborhoods, improving community safety and property values nearby.
Reduced Public Expenditure Fewer emergency shelter costs, reduced health care burdens from homelessness-related illnesses, and lower law enforcement costs.
Dignity and Stability for Individuals Stable housing improves mental health, employment prospects, child education outcomes, and family cohesion.
Pressure on Speculators Even the threat of confiscation or heavy taxation discourages speculative hoarding of housing stock, increasing affordable supply.
Reinforcement of Social Contract Signals that society prioritizes collective well-being over unaccountable private wealth accumulation.

Important Nuances and Counterarguments

While the benefits are compelling to supporters, such policies face serious criticism and practical hurdles:

  • Constitutional Property Rights: In countries like the U.S., the Fifth Amendment requires “just compensation” for takings. Confiscation without payment would likely face constitutional challenges.
  • Rule of Law and Due Process: Arbitrary seizure undermines legal certainty and property rights, potentially discouraging investment or home maintenance.
  • Administrative Complexity: Determining “vacancy” or “underutilization” requires robust oversight; abuses could lead to misuse or targeting of innocent owners.
  • Potential Disincentives: Owners might avoid renting (even at low rates) to avoid regulation or confiscation, worsening housing supply.
  • Political Feasibility: Strong opposition from real estate interests, homeowners’ groups, and libertarian ideologies can block adoption.

Therefore, most viable proposals do not advocate outright confiscation, but rather:

  • Compulsory purchase with fair market compensation
  • Heavy vacancy taxes (e.g., 50–200% of property value annually)
  • Mandatory rental obligations for long-term vacant units
  • Transfer of ownership to public housing authorities after repeated non-compliance

Conclusion

The underlying motivation for policies that repurpose vacant properties for the homeless is not about punishing property owners—it is about correcting systemic failures where housing is treated as a commodity rather than a human necessity. The supposed benefits include rapid, humane, and economical solutions to homelessness, revitalized communities, and a more just distribution of resources.

While full confiscation without compensation is legally and politically fraught in most democracies, progressive versions of the policy—using incentives, taxes, and eminent domain with compensation—are emerging as viable, humane tools in cities facing severe housing crises. The goal is not to abolish private property, but to recalibrate its social responsibilities.
